questions.q: What distinguishes short-term memory from long-term memory in this lesson?
options: Short-term memory is always more accurate than long-term memory
Short-term memory sits inside the current context window; long-term memory is stored externally and retrieved back into context on demand
Long-term memory is free and short-term memory requires a database
There is no real difference between the two
questions.explain: Short-term memory is this session's history inside the context window, while long-term memory lives outside it in storage and is pulled back in by retrieval when relevant.

questions.q: In the example memory record ({user_id, fact, source_turn, confidence, saved_at}), what is the purpose of the confidence and saved_at fields?
options: They are required by every JSON object and have no specific purpose here
They determine the user's subscription tier
They replace the need for a user_id field
They support staleness handling — judging whether an old stored fact is still trustworthy
questions.explain: The lesson explains these fields exist specifically to support staleness handling, since a long-term fact can become wrong over time and nothing automatically rechecks it.

questions.q: According to the lesson, which kind of fact is the better candidate for long-term storage rather than short-term memory?
options: A stated user preference that should persist and be useful in future, unrelated sessions
A calculation being worked out only for the current task
The exact wording of the current turn's question
A document the user just pasted in for this one task
questions.explain: The lesson identifies durable facts worth keeping across sessions — like a stated preference — as good candidates for long-term storage, while task-scoped content stays short-term.

questions.q: Why does short-term memory never face the 'staleness' problem that long-term memory does?
options: Short-term memory is always encrypted
Short-term memory is stored in a vector database that auto-updates
Short-term memory disappears at the end of the session, so there's no old version left around to contradict a newer fact
Staleness only applies to tool schemas, not memory
questions.explain: Because short-term memory is gone when the session ends, there's no persisted old fact that could become outdated and contradict current information — a risk unique to long-term storage.

questions.q: Once a long-term memory record is retrieved back into context for a new session, what does the lesson say applies to it?
options: It is exempt from the context window's token budget
It still has to fit the token budget and competes for a position in the window, like any other context
It automatically gets placed in the middle of the context window
It replaces the system prompt entirely
questions.explain: The lesson ties retrieval back to the budgeting (Lesson 13) and ordering (Lesson 15) concepts covered earlier in the chapter — a retrieved memory is still ordinary context once it's back in the window.
